title: Kayutangan as a Residential Center of Malang in the 20th Century
content: The Kayutangan settlement in the 20th century was not only shaped by rows of old houses, narrow alleys, and its proximity to the commercial center of Malang City, but also by the relationship between domestic space, economic activities, and family history. Rumah Rindu demonstrates how a house functions beyond a mere dwelling. The building became a space for production, inheritance, storage of old objects, and a vessel of intergenerational memory. The name "Rumah Rindu" does not refer to longing or nostalgia, but rather to the local term for wooden clog sandals. The identity of the house was thus born from the economic activities of its inhabitants, particularly the wooden sandal-making business run by Haji Nur Rohim since around the 1950s. Today, the Kayutangan settlement has become one of the most representative historical spaces in Malang City, showcasing the evolution and dynamics of urban residential development from the colonial era to the present day. The existence of twelve houses studied in this section affirms that Kayutangan is not merely a passive expanse of old buildings, but rather a living ecosystem that grew organically through complex interactions between architecture, kinship ties, types of occupation, trading activities, access to education, religious life, and population mobility. These houses grew within alleys connected to the Kayutangan trading corridor, Pasar Talun, Pasar Besar, places of worship, river streams, and the city road network. The intensive physical proximity between residential areas and centers of socio-economic activity ultimately gave birth to the spatial uniqueness of the area, where the boundary between private domestic space and public space in Kayutangan has always been flexible, fluid, and intertwined.

title: Rumah Rindu
content: Rumah Rindu in Kayutangan demonstrates how a 20th-century urban house functioned not only as a residence, but also as a space for production, family inheritance, storage of old objects, and the formation of intergenerational memory. The name "Rumah Rindu" derives from the local term for wooden clog sandals produced by Haji Nur Rohim since around the 1950s, so the house's identity is closely linked to the family's economic activities. Architecturally, this house retains a number of old elements, such as teak wood doors and windows, roof tiles, turn locks, and textured glass, although some parts have been adjusted, including changes to the roof construction to address leaks and expand space. Its spatial layout also shows a close relationship between domestic and economic functions, as the back area and attic were once used for sanding, painting, varnishing, and assembling sandals with the involvement of family members and neighbors. Various heirlooms, such as a radio, teak cabinet, table, loudspeaker, plates initialed "HNR," and two pairs of rindu sandals, now serve as material archives recording the history of the business, consumption patterns, mobility, and the family's social life. The story of Haji Nur Rohim and his familyâ€”including connections to the dokar (horse-drawn carriage) business, experiences of struggle around 1945, and the hajj journey by sea route in 1971â€”further strengthens the house's position as a repository of Kayutangan's social history. Currently, Bu Nunuk, as the youngest child, maintains the house and its various heirlooms with the principle of eman (reluctance to discard), while the division of the house among heirs reflects values of justice and family protection summarized in the Javanese expression "elek-elek o, supaya ora kudanan lan ora kepanasan" (however humble, so as not to be rained on or exposed to heat). Thus, Rumah Rindu demonstrates that the preservation of heritage houses in Kayutangan takes place through a combination of physical adaptation, continuity of function, family memory, and intergenerational responsibility.

title: Rumah D'Penghulu
content: Rumah D'Penghulu is a domestic building estimated to have been established since the 1910sâ€“1920s and has a strong connection to the penghulu (Islamic marriage official) profession carried out hereditarily by the owner's family. Besides serving as a residence, this house once functioned as the penghulu service office of Malang City before the establishment of KUA (Office of Religious Affairs), so that domestic space and public service space were united in one building. Traces of colonial architecture are still visible in the facade composition, upper ornaments, and the elongated room arrangement from the public area in front to the domestic space at the back. The spacious yard or latar ombo became an important element as it functioned as a playground, gathering place, economic activity space, music community venue, and even film production site. As times changed, the front part of the house was repeatedly adjusted for economic functions, from a grocery store in the 1980s to a food stall after the pandemic, while the main structure of the building was maintained. The living room formerly served as the center of penghulu activities, including receiving prospective brides and grooms, marriage ceremonies, and the jomblokan tradition, before administrative functions ended around 1969. The addition of an upper floor around 2000 shows a form of adaptation to family needs without significantly changing the main spatial layout of the ground floor. Although most of the old furniture has been taken by heirs, the house is maintained as a rumah punden (ancestral house) jointly owned by the family. Today, the building's value no longer rests on the formal function of the penghulu, but on the continuity of family memory, social activities of residents, and the ever-changing use of space, so that Rumah D'Penghulu remains a living part of the social history and development of the Kayutangan settlement.

title: Rumah Dawet Ireng
content: Rumah Dawet Ireng, owned by Bu Niken, is an old city house estimated to have stood since the colonial era. The determination of this building's history is primarily based on three types of information: family memory and local oral tradition, observation of old architectural elements that still survive, and administrative traces on water and electricity connections. Based on family oral accounts, this house was once inhabited by an Indian community, then an Arab family, before being purchased by Bu Niken's parents around 1984â€“1985. Information about these early periods is not yet supported by complete ownership documents, so it should be understood as a historical reconstruction based on family memory. Meanwhile, the existence of thick walls made of limestone, sand, and brick, old doors and windows, patterned cement tiles, wooden structures, roof tiles, and an old well provide material evidence regarding the age and character of the older building. The traces of the name Nyonya Zukrah on the water connection and Suweprapto on the electricity meter also provide administrative clues about previous inhabitants or owners, although they are not sufficient to compile a complete ownership sequence. Several changes were made during Bu Niken's family period, particularly widening the front section, bathroom renovation, and the addition of room dividers, while most of the main structure was maintained. Furniture from the Indian and Arab inhabitants is no longer found because the house was empty when purchased, so the current interior history narrative is more related to Bu Niken's family, who were previously active in trade along the Kayutangan corridor. Currently, the front room is used for the dawet ireng (black grass jelly drink) business, so the house once again serves a dual function as both residence and economic space. Thus, the history of Rumah Dawet Ireng can be understood as the result of cross-reading between oral sources, material architectural evidence, administrative traces, and family history, which together reveal changes in function and the continuity of house life in the Kayutangan area.

title: Rumah Jacoeb
content: Rumah Jacoeb is one of the old houses in Kayutangan that records the history of migration, family life, and the development of urban society in Malang in the early 20th century. Based on family memory, this house has been inhabited by Jacoeb Sutan Chaniago, a Minangkabau migrant from West Sumatra, since around 1920, although the identity of the original builder is no longer known. Historical information about the house primarily comes from family oral accounts, the existence of old photographs and certificates, objects still preserved, and the continuity of space usage from generation to generation. Architecturally, the house has an elongated pattern with a guest reception room in front, two bedrooms, a dining room, kitchen, bathroom, and a side area for drying clothes. The front section has not undergone major changes and still retains its distinctive element of a wall resembling a permanent bench that was formerly used as a table and seat for receiving guests, so the facade functions as a semi-open social space. The original floor from the front room to the dining room, teak wood chairs, and a number of family objects strengthen the material continuity of the house. The Ngarai Sianok painting is the most symbolically important object as it connects the domestic space in Kayutangan with the family's homeland in Minangkabau and represents the geographical memory of a migrant. Some of Jacoeb's personal archives are no longer found, while ownership documents are held by family members in Jakarta, so the current reconstruction of the building's history relies more on oral sources, photographs, visual objects, and family memory. Jacoeb's career at City Hall, his involvement in the Muhammadiyah environment, Azizah's economic activities in clothing trade, and the house's function as a stopover for relatives from Sumatra show that this building became part of the migration, employment, education, and trade network in Kayutangan. The house is now maintained by Ibu Silfi as Jacoeb's granddaughter and is still understood as a rumah punden, a center of family bonds that maintains the continuity of intergenerational memory even though the heirs have scattered across various cities.

title: Rumah Jengki
content: Rumah Jengki in Kayutangan is a post-independence building erected in 1960 by the owner's family with the services of Ir. Daryo from Surabaya, replacing the previous simple house that was considered no longer adequate for the large family. Historical information about the building primarily comes from family memory regarding the construction process, the designer's identity, the origins of the inhabitants, and the continuity of space and furniture usage. Architecturally, this house is understood as part of the Jengki style that developed after independence and displays a character different from colonial architecture, particularly through the asymmetrical facade composition, a gable roof with two differently-lengthed planes, and distinctive window opening shapes. The main spatial layout has remained relatively unchanged since the beginning; rooms, kitchen, roof, and windows remain in their original positions, while renovations were only carried out on a limited basis, such as layering new floors over old materials. The house interior was designed to accommodate a large family that once numbered about thirteen people, and changes in room function were carried out flexibly without dismantling the main structure. Currently, part of the house is used as a food and beverage business, while other parts continue to function as a residence, workspace, and place of worship. The Indian and Javanese dishes served reflect the family background formed from the meeting of Indian and Javanese descendants. Old furniture, such as wall clocks and various furnishings inherited from the owner's grandfather and father, are maintained not as sacred objects, but as part of family memory. Maintenance is carried out gradually to address wall dampness and wood decay without changing the original form of the building. Thus, Rumah Jengki is not only a family residence but also material evidence of post-independence architectural development in Kayutangan as well as an educational space that introduces the Jengki style through the building's form, family history, and the daily activities of its inhabitants.

title: Rumah Mbah Ndut
content: Rumah Mbah Ndut is an old family house in Kayutangan estimated to have been built around 1923 and continuously inhabited by successive generations to this day. Historical information about the building primarily comes from family memory, continuity of space usage, inherited objects, and physical changes that can still be traced in the structure of the house. Architecturally, this house retains its gable roof form, main building composition, large beams, and room arrangement consisting of a living room, family room, two bedrooms, kitchen, bathroom, and toilet. Although ceiling materials, battens, and rafters have been replaced several times due to damage, the basic form of the building has been maintained. The side path of the house also has an important social function as it was formerly used by children to avoid passing in front of guests, so the spatial layout also shaped the family's etiquette practices. Several room additions were made at the back to accommodate the growing number of inhabitants without changing the front facade. The house interior still stores various inherited objects, such as a buffet, plates, food containers, old school bags, family photographs, a keris, and a spear, which record domestic history as well as possible connections to import trade networks. Family photographs arranged according to lineage strengthen the house's function as an intergenerational memory storage space. In the family's understanding, this house was not merely inherited, but dinggeniâ€”inhabited and guarded as a rumah punden (ancestral house) jointly owned that should not be sold or arbitrarily altered. In the present day, the front room has undergone a change in function from a grocery store to a coffee shop serving residents and tourists. This change shows that Rumah Mbah Ndut remains alive through economic and social adaptation, while the architectural form, inherited objects, family etiquette, and collective memory remain the basis for the continuity of its identity.

title: Rumah Nyi Aisyah
content: Rumah Nyi Aisyah is an old family house in Kayutangan that has functioned as both a residence and a business space since around the 1920s. Historical information about the building primarily comes from family memory, continuity of lineage, space usage, and the existence of old furniture that still survives. The house naming refers to Nyi Aisyah, a descendant of Hasan Thaib, a migrant from Ciamis who settled in Kayutangan before the 1920s and divided his land among his children, thus forming a network of family housing in the surrounding area. Architecturally, the house has a gable roof and a relatively fixed room arrangement, while changes have mostly occurred in materials due to damage, such as replacement of roof tiles, rafters, gutters, and the addition of wall coatings to address dampness and leaks. The front section has long been connected to economic activity; during Nyi Aisyah's time, there was a service opening for selling beef, while the kitchen was used for food processing, including dendeng (dried meat). Today, this economic function continues in the form of cookies production with modern equipment, so the house maintains the connection between domestic space and business activities. The interior still stores cabinets, dining tables, buffets, and old mirrors that serve as intergenerational memory connectors, although they are not treated as sacred objects. The house has also never been sold or rented to outsiders, but has been continuously inhabited by family descendants and understood as a rumah punden. Family gatherings held periodically to prevent kepaten obor (extinguishing of the family torch) show that the house is not merely a physical asset, but also a center for maintaining kinship relations. Thus, Rumah Nyi Aisyah demonstrates the continuity between family heritage, architectural adaptation, and household economic changes in the development of Kayutangan from the 20th century to the present.

title: Rumah Nyak Abbas Akub
content: Rumah Nyak Abbas Akup is an old family house in Kayutangan that records the migration history of an Acehnese family, kinship networks, and residential adaptation in a colonial urban environment. Based on family memory, this building was estimated to have been erected around the 1920s by Nyak Akup, Nyak Abbas's father, after the family settled in Kayutangan around 1918â€“1920. Historical information about the house primarily comes from family oral tradition, continuity of lineage, surviving building structures, and family objects and stories that have been passed down. Typologically, the house is part of a series of four family dwellings with an elongated pattern, two main buildings on the north and south sides, and a central corridor that formerly still partially used klenengan construction from walls and woven bamboo. Its spatial layout places the front room as a guest reception area and a symbol of the head of family's authority, while the corridor functions as a connector between rooms and between family members. Several changes were made to openings, the roof, and the corridor to adjust to the inhabitants' needs, while the main structure was maintained. Most of Nyak Akup's original furniture has been dispersed among the heirs, so not all objects currently displayed are direct family heirlooms. The rencong and traditional headcover that, according to family memory, were brought by Nyak Akup from Aceh were once strong markers of the family's genealogical origins, although the whereabouts of these objects are no longer known. Nyak Akup's history as an Acehnese migrant working in Malang, and his children's journeys into press, forestry, office work, and the arts, demonstrate the family's social mobility. The name Nyak Abbas later became more attached to the house due to his role in the world of art and film. Today, Pak Endias develops part of the house as an art space containing paintings, photographs, recycled objects, and plans for a film screening room, so the building remains alive as a residence, family memory space, and medium for preserving cross-generational cultural identity.

title: Rumah Pak Udin
content: Rumah Pak Udin is an old family house in Kayutangan estimated to have been built around 1930 by his grandparents after settling in Malang. Historical information about the building primarily comes from family memory, continuity of lineage, the existence of old architectural elements, inherited furniture, and changes in room function over time. Typologically, this house can be understood as a local urban house that adapted visual elements of colonial architecture, particularly from houses in the Jalan Ijen area, visible in the grilles, frames, and front composition. The main structure of the house has been relatively maintained, while changes were made on a limited basis to the fence, roof, kitchen, bathroom, drying area, and the addition of a tent to support the warung (food stall) function. Old elements such as cement floors, frames, roof timber, and an aged well remain an important part of the building's character. The well, approximately twelve to fifteen meters deep, records the phase when Kayutangan households still relied on independent water sources before being connected to the PDAM (municipal water) network. The interior also stores a large clock and a number of furnishings maintained per family instructions not to sell them, while the mushola (prayer room) serves as a marker of the family's religious tradition continuity. The history of the inhabitants shows a close relationship with the city's economy: Pak Udin's grandfather managed dokar (horse-drawn carriage) rentals, his grandmother traded meat at Pasar Besar, while his father worked as an aannemer (building contractor). Pak Udin began occupying the house around 1996 and maintained it as a family heirloom, although ownership has now been formalized in his name. Since around 2023, the front has been used as a warung in response to increasing tourist visits, after the family had also been involved in clothing trade at Pasar Besar. This house was also used as a filming location for the movie Yowis Ben 2. Thus, Rumah Pak Udin demonstrates the continuity between the history of an immigrant family, economic activities, religious traditions, architectural adaptation, and changes in room function in the development of Kayutangan from the 20th century to the present.

title: Rumah 1870
content: Rumah 1870 is an old family house in Kayutangan that records the relationship between permanent housing, family heritage, trading activities, and the development of area tourism. The basis of this building's historical information is relatively strong because it comes not only from family memory and old photographs, but is also supported by a gift reinforcement letter dated September 26, 1938, which mentions a tiled house with a kitchen, bathroom, well, and standing on land of approximately 13 Ã— 88 meters. In family documents, the building is referred to as rumah gedung tegel or omah gedong, a term that distinguishes it from the board, wood, and woven bamboo houses still commonly found at that time. Although the name "1870" is used as the house's identity, this number is not a verified construction year, but rather derives from an architectural style reading by Budi Fathoni, so it cannot be used as a definitive basis for dating the building. This house was inherited through the family line of Siti Aminah, daughter of Haji Marzuki, and was subsequently maintained so as not to pass to outside parties. Its spatial layout follows the elongated shape of the land, with the front section as a reception area and the middle-back for domestic functions. The old well shows independence in water supply before the development of the city water network, while the front yard also functioned as a play and social interaction space. The history of Atmokahar as an antique goods trader shaped the interior character, which was once filled with vases, plates, cabinets, and various collections, although most of these objects later dispersed among the heirs. Family photographs and the gift document now serve as important sources for maintaining the house's genealogical memory. In the present day, Rumah 1870 functions as a cafÃ© and part of Kayutangan's tourist attraction, so that the old domestic space has transformed into a meeting space between family, residents, and tourists. Thus, Rumah 1870 demonstrates the continuity between documentary evidence, inheritance history, family memory, and economic function adaptation in the development of Kayutangan.

title: Rumah Bu Kembar
content: Rumah Bu Kembar is an old family house in Kayutangan estimated to have been built in the early 20th century, around 1910â€“1920s, based on family genealogy, photo documentation, and its architectural character; the number "1800" once readable on the frame cannot serve as a dating basis as its condition has worn away. This house can be understood as an urban priyayi (Javanese aristocracy) family residence with Indis architectural influence, visible from the semi-open terrace, arched openings, tiled floors, high ceilings, ornamented doors, spacious work rooms, and linear room arrangement from front to back. Some front sections underwent changes for security reasons, particularly the enclosure of the terrace with additional doors and windows, but main elements such as tiles, doors, facade ornaments, and room arrangement have been largely maintained. An old well approximately fifteen meters deep, teak wood furniture, and traces of piano and violin use indicate the household life of an educated family in the past. The basis of this house's historical information is quite strong because besides relying on family memory, it is also supported by photo documentation made by Soekiswoso, which records changes in the facade, fence, yard, clothing, tennis activities, and family life over time. The name Rumah Bu Kembar refers to Ananingsih and Ananingsutji, twin sisters who chose not to marry in order to care for their mother, Sribanu, and both worked as teachers at SDK Sang Timur. The story of Ananingsih, remembered for encouraging Andy F. Noya to pursue journalism, further strengthens the social memory of this house. Today, the house remains a space for preserving family history through photographs, furniture, old architectural elements, and intergenerational memory, while representing the relationship between social status, women's education, family life, and the development of Kayutangan society in the 20th century.

title: Kedai Namsun
content: Kedai Namsun is an old building in the Kayutangan corridor that demonstrates the fusion of residential and commercial functions since the early 20th century. The basis of its historical information primarily comes from interviews, architectural element readings, and community memory regarding changes in building function; the oldest data mentioned relates to around 1924. Based on the facade form, geometric arrangement, vertical lines, and the composition of doors and windows, this building is estimated to have Art Deco characteristics, although this classification still requires stronger documentary support. A number of old elements, such as doors, stairs, display glass, and hoisting equipment on the upper floor, still serve as clues regarding past commercial and storage functions. Its spatial layout shows a division between the open front area for service and merchandise display and the more private back section and upper floor for residence and storage. Oral history indicates that the building was once used for photography activities, a Singer sewing machine shop, and Comcom ice production, thus reflecting changes in commodities and trading technology in Kayutangan. Although original furniture from each period is no longer complete, the pattern of commercial space usage continues to this day. The building now functions as a cafÃ©, with the front space used to receive visitors, while old architectural elements become part of the tourist experience. Thus, Kedai Namsun demonstrates the continuity of economic function in a single building, while also recording changes in consumption culture, technology, mobility, and urban life in Kayutangan throughout the 20th century.
